title: SQL in plain words
summary: Read the SQL Claude Code writes: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT to read data, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to change it.
youWillLearn: How to read any SQL statement as a sentence: verb, table, which rows
INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE for changing data, and why WHERE is the line to check
How the Supabase client maps to SQL, and why values go in as parameters

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.SQL: Structured Query Language: the language you use to ask a relational database for data or to change it.
glossary.query: One request written in SQL, like "give me Maya's notes, newest first".
glossary.declarative: You describe the result you want, and the system works out the steps to get it.
glossary.SELECT: The SQL verb that reads data and picks which columns to return.
glossary.WHERE: The part of a statement that decides which rows are affected, by a test each row must pass.
glossary.ORDER BY: Sorts the result by one or more columns, ascending (asc) or descending (desc).
glossary.LIMIT: Stops the result after a set number of rows.
glossary.INSERT: The SQL verb that adds new rows to a table.
glossary.UPDATE: The SQL verb that changes values in existing rows.
glossary.DELETE: The SQL verb that removes rows from a table, for good.
glossary.parameter: A placeholder like $1 in a query, filled with a value sent separately, so the value can never be read as SQL.
glossary.transaction: A group of writes that succeed or fail together. If one fails, Postgres undoes all of them.
glossary.SQL injection: An attack where user input is glued into a SQL string and runs as part of the command.

steps.title: Notely talks to its database in SQL
body: Notely's app server (the computer running its code) keeps every note in the database. To read or change notes, it sends the database a query written in SQL, the language databases understand.
On the right are three rows of the notes table. Two belong to Maya (user 7), one to Leo (user 8).

scene.caption: The app server, and three rows of the notes table it sends SQL to.

steps.title: A query you did not write
body: Claude Code writes most of Notely's SQL. For Maya's list it wrote select * from notes;. It runs without an error, and returns every row in the table. Maya's list now shows Leo's Trip plan.
You do not need to write SQL from memory. You do need to read it, because one missing line decides whose notes get touched.
changes: ~ Rows touched 0 → 3: every row in the table
~ Others' notes 0 → 1: Leo's Trip plan on Maya's screen

scene.caption: No filter: every row goes back, Leo's included.

steps.title: SQL reads like a sentence
body: SQL is declarative: you say what you want, not how to find it. Postgres, Notely's database, works out the how.
Most statements read like a sentence: a verb, a table, then which rows. select * from notes has a verb and a table, but no which rows. That missing part is the bug.

callout.text: Ordering at a restaurant. You say "the risotto, no cheese". You do not walk into the kitchen and tell the chef which pan to use.

changes: ~ App Server: we read its query as a sentence

scene.caption: Verb, table, which rows. The third part is missing.

steps.title: SELECT and WHERE: pick and filter
body: SELECT picks the columns. FROM names the table. WHERE keeps only the rows that pass a test.
Here Postgres checks each row: is user_id 7? Maya's rows pass, Leo's is skipped. select * means every column: handy while exploring, wasteful in app code.

code.caption: Keywords work in any case; lowercase is common.

changes: ~ Rows touched 3 → 2
~ Others' notes 1 → 0: Leo's row is skipped
~ App Server: the query now says which rows

scene.caption: WHERE user_id = 7 lets Maya's two rows through and skips Leo's.

steps.title: ORDER BY and LIMIT: newest first
body: Rows come back in no promised order. If order matters, say so. ORDER BY created_at desc sorts newest first; asc is oldest first.
LIMIT stops after a number of rows. Notely's "Latest" card shows only Maya's newest note, so the query stops after one.

code.code:
select title, created_at
from notes
where user_id = 7
order by created_at desc
limit 1;

changes: ~ Book ideas moves to the top: it is the newest
~ Groceries is cut by the limit
~ Rows touched 2 → 1

scene.caption: Sorted newest first, then cut after one row.

steps.title: INSERT: add a new row
body: INSERT adds a row. You list the columns, then the values in the same order. Columns you skip get their default, like a fresh id or the current time.
Add returning and Postgres hands back the new row's values, so the app can open the new note right away.

callout.text: Some writes belong together, like a note and its tag links. Wrap them in a transaction (begin; … commit;). If one statement fails, Postgres undoes all of them.

changes: + Pitch deck: a new row for Maya
~ Every other row back to normal

scene.caption: A new row joins the table. Postgres fills in its id and time.

steps.title: UPDATE: change the rows that match
body: UPDATE changes values in existing rows. SET says what changes, WHERE says which rows.
Point the WHERE at the primary key, and exactly one row changes. Point it at something broad, like a title, and every matching row changes, whoever owns it.

code.code:
update notes
set title = 'Groceries (Sat)'
where id = 101;  -- 101 is Groceries

callout.text: Before running an UPDATE or DELETE by hand, run the same WHERE as a SELECT. If it returns exactly the rows you expect, swap the verb.

changes: ~ Groceries → Groceries (Sat): one row, picked by its id
~ Pitch deck settles in

scene.caption: WHERE id = 101 picks exactly one row to change.

steps.title: DELETE without WHERE empties the table
body: DELETE removes the rows that match the WHERE. No undo, no trash folder, unless you build one (lesson 4).
delete from notes where id = 102; removes one note. Lose the last part and you get delete from notes;: valid SQL that removes every note, for every user. All two million.

callout.text: Know where your backups are before you need them: check your Supabase project's backup settings now, not after a bad delete.

changes: ~ Every row turns red: no WHERE means every row matches
~ Rows touched 1 → 2,000,000
~ Others' notes 0 → all

scene.caption: No WHERE means every row in the table matches.

steps.title: The same query, from Notely's code
body: Notely's code uses the Supabase client, a library that builds the SQL for you. Each method maps to a word you know: .select(), .eq() for where, .order(), .limit().
When you write raw SQL in code, pass values as parameters. Pasting user input into the SQL string is how SQL injection happens.

code.code:
const { data, error } = await supabase
  .from('notes')
  .select('title, created_at')
  .eq('user_id', userId)
  .order('created_at', { ascending: false })
  .limit(20);
code.caption: Same as: select … where user_id = $1 order by created_at desc limit 20.

callout.text: For each query Claude Code writes, find the verb and the WHERE. Does every UPDATE and DELETE target an id? Is user input passed as a parameter, never inside a template string with ${...}? Try risky statements on a test database first.

changes: ~ Rows back to normal: that delete never ran
~ Rows touched 2,000,000 → 3: Maya's notes only
~ Others' notes all → 0
+ Maya's three rows flow back to the App Server

scene.caption: Client methods become one SQL query: Maya's notes, newest first.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: SQL is a sentence: verb, table, which rows. SELECT reads, WHERE filters, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT caps. INSERT adds, UPDATE changes, DELETE removes.
When you review Claude Code's SQL, look hardest at the WHERE. It decides whose data gets touched.
changes: ~ All rows calm: a query that says exactly which rows it means

scene.caption: Verb, table, which rows: read every query this way.

quiz.question: Which query returns Maya's 10 newest notes? (Maya is user 7.)

options.why: No WHERE and no ORDER BY: any 10 notes from any users, in no promised order.

options.text: select * from notes where user_id = 7 order by created_at asc limit 10;
options.why: asc sorts oldest first, so this returns her 10 oldest notes.

options.text: select * from notes where user_id = 7 order by created_at desc limit 10;
options.why: Filter to Maya, sort newest first, then stop after 10. Verb, table, which rows, order, cap.

quiz.question: Claude Code wrote update notes set pinned = true where title = 'Groceries'; for Maya's "pin" button. What is wrong?

options.text: It pins every note titled Groceries, including other users' notes.
options.why: The WHERE matches by title, which is not unique. Target the note's id (and check the owner) so exactly one row changes.

options.text: true should be written as the string 'true'.
options.why: pinned is a yes/no column, so true is correct. The problem is which rows match.

options.text: An UPDATE needs a LIMIT 1 at the end.
options.why: Postgres does not allow LIMIT on UPDATE. The safe fix is a WHERE that matches only the row you mean.

quiz.question: A search route builds `select * from notes where title = '${search}'` from what the user typed. What do you ask Claude Code to change?

options.text: Add limit 20 so the query stays fast.
options.why: Speed is not the danger. Typed input can end the string and add its own SQL.

options.text: Pass search as a parameter, or use the client's .eq().
options.why: Parameters send the value separately from the SQL, so it can never run as code. That closes the SQL injection hole.

options.text: Write the SQL keywords in uppercase.
options.why: Case makes no difference to Postgres, and none to the injection risk.

takeaways: Read SQL as a sentence: verb, table, which rows.
Without ORDER BY there is no promised order. Add LIMIT to any list a screen shows.
Every UPDATE and DELETE needs a WHERE that targets exactly the rows you mean, ideally by id.
Test a risky WHERE as a SELECT first.
User input goes in as a parameter, never pasted into the SQL string.
